decks.title: The Periodic Table — Part 1: Early classifications and the periodic law
goals: Show that a given set of elements forms a Dobereiner triad and state Newlands' law of octaves with one limitation
State Mendeleev's periodic law with its merits and limitations
Explain how the use of atomic number removed the anomalies of Mendeleev's table

slides.heading: Sorting the elements
slides.body_md: Part 1 — as more elements were found, scientists looked for **patterns** that would sort them into families.

visual.alt: Flow of four steps in the history of the periodic table

slides.narration: Chemists found more and more elements and wanted to sort them. We follow four steps: triads, octaves, the periodic law of Mendeleev, and finally the use of atomic number.

slides.heading: Dobereiner's triads
slides.body_md: A **triad** is a group of **three elements with similar properties**. When they are arranged by atomic mass, the mass of the **middle** element is about the **mean** of the other two.

visual.alt: Table of two Dobereiner triads with the mean of the first and third atomic masses

slides.narration: Dobereiner noticed groups of three elements that behave alike. In each group the middle element has an atomic mass close to the average of the other two. Lithium, sodium and potassium form such a triad, and so do chlorine, bromine and iodine.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is it a triad?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The atomic masses of calcium, strontium and barium are 40, 88 and 137. Do they form a Dobereiner triad?

**Step 1.** Mean of the first and third: $(40 + 137) \div 2 = 88.5$.

**Step 2.** Compare with the middle element: 88. The difference is only **0.5**.

**Step 3.** The three elements also have similar properties, so they **form a triad**.

visual.alt: Table comparing the mean mass with the mass of strontium

slides.narration: Add the masses of calcium and barium and divide by two. The mean is eighty eight and a half, which is very close to strontium at eighty eight. The three metals also behave alike, so they form a triad.

slides.heading: Quick check: a triad
slides.body_md: Both the numbers and the properties matter.

visual.alt: Atomic masses of sulphur, selenium and tellurium

slides.narration: Sulphur, selenium and tellurium have similar properties. Which statement about their atomic masses supports a triad?

slides.heading: Newlands' law of octaves
slides.body_md: Newlands arranged the elements in the order of **increasing atomic mass**. He found that **every eighth element** had properties like the first, like the notes of a musical scale.

rows: Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Na

visual.alt: Table showing the eighth element in three counts in the law of octaves

slides.narration: Newlands listed the elements by atomic mass. Starting at lithium and counting to the eighth element gives sodium, which is like lithium. Starting at sodium gives potassium, and starting at fluorine gives chlorine.

slides.heading: Limitations of Newlands' law
slides.body_md: The law worked only up to **calcium**. After that, elements did not repeat every eighth place.

rows: Held good only up to calcium
Heavier elements did not show the repeating pattern
Some columns had elements with different properties
Noble gases found later did not fit the octaves

visual.alt: Table of three limitations of the law of octaves

slides.narration: The law of octaves worked only up to calcium. Beyond that, elements with unlike properties were forced into the same column. There was also no room for new elements, such as the noble gases found later.

slides.heading: Mendeleev's periodic law
slides.body_md: The **properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses**. Mendeleev arranged the elements in **groups** (vertical columns) and **periods** (horizontal rows).

rows: Left for elements not yet discovered

visual.alt: Table summarising the features of Mendeleev's periodic table

slides.narration: Mendeleev stated that the properties of elements repeat at intervals when they are arranged by atomic mass. His table had groups going down and periods going across. Where no known element fitted, he left a gap.

slides.heading: Merits and limitations

rows: Gaps predicted new elements: eka-aluminium (found as gallium) and eka-silicon (found as germanium)
Hydrogen could not be given a fixed place
Atomic masses of some elements were corrected
Some elements were placed out of order of atomic mass
Elements of a group had similar properties
No separate place for isotopes of an element
The group number helped to predict the valency of an element

visual.alt: Table of merits and limitations of Mendeleev's table

slides.narration: Mendeleev left gaps and predicted the properties of the missing elements. Eka-aluminium was later found as gallium, and eka-silicon as germanium. But hydrogen had no fixed place, isotopes had no place, and some elements were out of order of atomic mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: an element out of order
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Tellurium (atomic mass 127.6) is placed before iodine (126.9) in Mendeleev's table, although it is heavier. How can this be explained?

**Step 1.** Difference in mass: 127.6 − 126.9 = **0.7**; tellurium is heavier.

**Step 2.** Mendeleev placed iodine after tellurium because iodine resembles chlorine and bromine, so the **order of atomic mass was broken**.

**Step 3.** Atomic numbers are 52 and 53: arranged by atomic number the order is correct.

visual.alt: Atomic mass and atomic number of tellurium and iodine

slides.narration: Tellurium is slightly heavier than iodine, yet it comes before iodine in the table. This broke the rule of increasing atomic mass. Atomic numbers are fifty two and fifty three, and in that order the problem disappears.

slides.heading: Atomic number and the modern periodic law
slides.body_md: Moseley showed that the **atomic number** (number of protons) is the true basis. The **modern periodic law**: properties of elements are a periodic function of their **atomic numbers**.

visual.alt: Table showing how atomic number removes anomalies of the earlier table

slides.narration: Moseley discovered that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the basis. Arranged by atomic number, tellurium and iodine, and argon and potassium, all fall in the right order. Isotopes have the same atomic number, so they share one place.

slides.body_md: What do the elements follow now?

visual.alt: The basis of the modern periodic law

slides.narration: On what basis are the elements arranged in the modern periodic law?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Dobereiner: in a triad the middle mass is about the mean of the first and third.
Newlands: every eighth element repeats; it worked only up to calcium.
Mendeleev: properties are periodic functions of atomic masses; gaps predicted elements.
Modern law: properties are periodic functions of atomic numbers; this removed the anomalies.

visual.alt: Summary table of four classifications of elements

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Dobereiner found triads and Newlands found octaves. Mendeleev gave the periodic law and left gaps. Atomic number then replaced atomic mass as the basis, which solved the remaining anomalies.

slides.heading: The modern table
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **18 groups** across and **7 periods** down. The position of an element tells you its electron arrangement.

visual.alt: Flow from electronic configuration to period and group and then properties

slides.narration: The modern table has eighteen groups across and seven periods down. If you know the electron arrangement of an atom, you can find its period and group, and then predict its properties.

slides.heading: The table in outline
slides.body_md: The first 20 elements are named. Groups 1 and 2 are on the left, **transition elements** in groups 3 to 12, and groups 13 to 18 on the right.

slides.narration: The periods are of different lengths: two, eight, eight, eighteen, eighteen, thirty two and thirty two elements. In all, they add up to one hundred and eighteen elements.

slides.heading: Finding the period and the group
slides.body_md: The **period** equals the **number of shells**. The **group** is the number of outer electrons for groups 1 and 2, and **10 + outer electrons** for 3 to 8 outer electrons (group 18 for a full shell).

visual.alt: Table of period and group for five atoms from their configurations

slides.narration: Count the shells for the period. For the group, use the outer electrons: one or two give group one or two, and three to eight outer electrons give group thirteen to eighteen. Sodium is in period three, group one. Sulphur is in period three, group sixteen.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: locating an element
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An atom has atomic number 19. Find its period and group.

**Step 1.** Configuration: **2, 8, 8, 1**.

**Step 2.** Number of shells = **4**, so period **4**.

**Step 3.** Outer electrons = **1**, so group **1**: an alkali metal (potassium).

visual.alt: Period and group of the element of atomic number nineteen

slides.narration: Write the configuration, two, eight, eight, one. There are four shells, so the period is four. There is one outer electron, so the group is one. This is potassium, an alkali metal.

slides.heading: Group 1: the alkali metals
slides.body_md: Lithium, sodium, potassium and others have **one valence electron**, which they lose to form **M⁺** ions. They are soft, reactive metals, and **reactivity increases down the group**.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from configuration to properties
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Element X has the configuration 2, 8, 8, 2. State its group and period, the ion it forms and its reactivity compared with magnesium.

**Step 1.** 4 shells and 2 outer electrons: **period 4, group 2**.

**Step 2.** It loses 2 electrons: ion **X²⁺**.

**Step 3.** It is below magnesium in group 2, so it is **more reactive** than magnesium. (X is calcium.)

visual.alt: Table of the position and properties of element X

slides.narration: Four shells give period four and two outer electrons give group two. The element loses two electrons to form an ion with a charge of two plus. It lies below magnesium, so it is more reactive. It is calcium.

slides.heading: Group 17: the halogens
slides.body_md: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine have **seven valence electrons** and gain one to form **X⁻** ions. They exist as **two-atom molecules** and **reactivity decreases down the group**.

visual.alt: Table of the state and colour of the four halogens at room temperature

slides.narration: The halogens have seven outer electrons and gain one to form negative ions. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid. The ability to gain an electron, and so the reactivity, decreases down the group.

slides.heading: Group 18: the noble gases
slides.body_md: Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon have a **full outer shell**: a duplet for helium and an octet for the rest. They are **inert, single-atom gases**.

visual.alt: Table of three noble gases with their configurations and uses

slides.narration: Noble gases already have full outer shells, so they do not gain, lose or share electrons. That is why they are inert. They exist as single atoms. Helium fills balloons, neon lights signs and argon fills electric bulbs.

sections.heading: 1. Early classifications: Dobereiner's triads and Newlands' law of octaves
sections.body_md:
**Dobereiner's triads.** Dobereiner grouped elements in threes, called **triads**, with similar properties. When the three are arranged by atomic mass, the mass of the **middle** element is approximately the **mean** of the masses of the other two.

| Triad (first, middle, third) | Atomic masses | Mean of the first and third |
|---|---|---|
| Lithium, sodium, potassium | 7, 23, 39 | 23 |
| Calcium, strontium, barium | 40, 88, 137 | 88.5 |
| Chlorine, bromine, iodine | 35.5, 80, 127 | 81.25 |
| Sulphur, selenium, tellurium | 32, 79, 128 | 80 |

The mean is close to, not always equal to, the middle mass. The numbers alone are not enough: the three elements must also behave alike (carbon, nitrogen and oxygen fit the arithmetic but are unlike). Only a few triads could be found, which limited the idea.

**Newlands' law of octaves.** Newlands arranged the elements in the order of **increasing atomic mass** and found that **every eighth element has properties similar to the first**, like the eighth note of a musical scale. Counting lithium as the first, the eighth is sodium; from sodium it is potassium; from fluorine it is chlorine.

**Limitations:** the law held good only up to **calcium**; elements with unlike properties were put in the same column; there was no place for elements discovered later, such as the noble gases.

key_terms.definition_md: A group of three elements with similar properties in which the atomic mass of the middle element is about the mean of the other two.
When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass, every eighth element has properties similar to the first.

sections.heading: 2. Mendeleev's periodic law
sections.body_md:
**Mendeleev's periodic law:** the **properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses**.

He arranged the elements in **groups** (vertical columns, I to VIII) and **periods** (horizontal rows), left **gaps** for elements not yet discovered and predicted their properties.

**Merits**
- Gaps were left and properties predicted: **eka-aluminium** was discovered as **gallium** and **eka-silicon** as **germanium**, with properties close to those predicted.
- The atomic masses of some elements were corrected to fit.
- Elements of a group have similar properties, and the group number helped to predict valency.

**Limitations**
- **Hydrogen** could not be given a fixed place (it resembles both group 1 and group 17).
- Some elements were placed **out of the order of atomic mass**, for example tellurium (127.6) before iodine (126.9), cobalt (58.9) before nickel (58.7); argon (39.9) is placed before potassium (39.1) in the modern order.
- There was **no separate place for isotopes**, which have different atomic masses but the same properties.
- The noble gases, found later, had no place.

Atomic masses are rounded; books quote slightly different values and some give a different number of predicted elements.

sections.heading: 4. The modern periodic table
sections.body_md:
The modern table has **18 groups** (vertical columns) and **7 periods** (horizontal rows).

- **Period** = the number of shells in the atom. The periods have 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 elements (118 in all; period 7 is completed by recently made elements).
- **Group**: elements of a group have the same number of **valence (outer) electrons**. Groups 1 and 2: group number = outer electrons. Groups 13 to 18: group number = 10 + outer electrons. Helium (2 outer electrons) is in group 18.

| Element | Atomic number | Configuration | Period | Group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lithium (Li) | 3 | 2, 1 | 2 | 1 |
| Beryllium (Be) | 4 | 2, 2 | 2 | 2 |
| Carbon (C) | 6 | 2, 4 | 2 | 14 |
| Sodium (Na) | 11 | 2, 8, 1 | 3 | 1 |
| Aluminium (Al) | 13 | 2, 8, 3 | 3 | 13 |
| Sulphur (S) | 16 | 2, 8, 6 | 3 | 16 |
| Argon (Ar) | 18 | 2, 8, 8 | 3 | 18 |
| Potassium (K) | 19 | 2, 8, 8, 1 | 4 | 1 |
| Calcium (Ca) | 20 | 2, 8, 8, 2 | 4 | 2 |

- **Transition elements** are in **groups 3 to 12** (periods 4 to 7).
- **Inner transition elements** (the lanthanides and the actinides, 14 elements in each of the two rows) are placed in **two rows below** the main table, to keep it from becoming too wide. Books differ slightly on which elements to count in each row.
- Groups 1 and 2 and groups 13 to 18 are the main-group elements.

key_terms.definition_md: A horizontal row of the periodic table; its number is the number of shells in the atoms.
A vertical column of the periodic table; atoms in a group have the same number of valence electrons.

sections.heading: 5. Groups 1, 2, 17 and 18
sections.body_md:
Common properties follow from the number of valence electrons.

| Group | Name | Valence electrons | Ion formed | Trend down the group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) | 1 | M⁺ | Reactivity increases; melting point falls |
| 2 | Alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) | 2 | M²⁺ | Reactivity increases |
| 17 | Halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) | 7 | X⁻ | Reactivity decreases; boiling point rises |
| 18 | Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe) | 2 for He, 8 for the rest | none | Inert; boiling point rises |

- **Alkali metals** are soft, very reactive and stored under oil; they react with water to give hydrogen and an alkaline solution. Approximate melting points (°C): lithium 181, sodium 98, potassium 63, rubidium 39, caesium 28.
- **Alkaline earth metals** are harder and less reactive than the alkali metals of the same period.
- **Halogens** exist as two-atom molecules: fluorine (pale yellow gas), chlorine (greenish-yellow gas), bromine (reddish-brown liquid), iodine (dark grey solid giving violet vapour). Approximate boiling points (°C): fluorine -188, chlorine -34, bromine 59, iodine 184.
- **Noble gases** have a full outer shell, exist as single atoms and are inert. Uses: helium for balloons, neon for signs, argon for electric bulbs.

The values are approximate and books differ in the last digit.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying a triad needs only the mean to work: the properties must also be similar.
- Saying Newlands or Mendeleev used atomic numbers: they used atomic masses.
- Writing the modern periodic law with atomic mass.
- Giving the group of aluminium as 3 instead of 13, or sulphur as 6 instead of 16.
- Forgetting that helium has 2 outer electrons.
- Saying the halogens lose an electron, or that reactivity of the halogens increases down the group.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a law, a period or group number, or a name.
- 2 marks: a triad calculation with a conclusion, two merits or two limitations, a configuration with the position.
- 3 marks: positions of three elements; properties of a group related to valence electrons.
- 10-mark structured question: a data table or lettered table outline with parts of 2 to 4 marks: calculations of means, laws, positions, group trends.

cards.back_md: In a group of three similar elements arranged by atomic mass, the middle mass is about the mean of the other two.
Masses 7, 23, 39; mean of 7 and 39 is 23.
Masses 35.5, 80, 127; mean of the outer two is 81.25, close to 80.

cards.back_md: The three elements must also have similar properties.
When elements are arranged by increasing atomic mass, every eighth element has properties like the first.

cards.back_md: Sodium and potassium.
Held only up to calcium; unlike elements in a column; no place for the noble gases.
Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.
Gaps predicted gallium and germanium; some masses corrected; similar elements grouped.
Elements predicted by Mendeleev, later found as gallium and germanium.
Hydrogen had no fixed place; elements out of mass order; no place for isotopes or noble gases.

cards.back_md: Te 127.6 comes before I 126.9, yet Te is heavier.
Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

cards.back_md: Moseley.

cards.back_md: Te (52) comes before I (53); isotopes share one place.

questions.stem_md:
A student studies two sets of elements with similar properties. Set P: chlorine (35.5), bromine (80) and iodine (127). Set Q: sulphur (32), selenium (79) and tellurium (128). The numbers in brackets are atomic masses.

(a) Calculate the mean of the first and the third mass in each set. [4]

(b) State whether each set agrees with the rule of Dobereiner's triads, giving a reason. [2]

(c) State Dobereiner's law of triads. [2]

(d) Why could the idea of triads not be used to classify all the known elements? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Set P: (35.5 + 127) ÷ 2 = **81.25**. Set Q: (32 + 128) ÷ 2 = **80**.

**(b)** **Both** agree: each mean is **close to the middle mass** (80 and 79) and the elements in each set have similar properties.

**(c)** Elements with similar properties, grouped in threes by atomic mass, have a **middle member whose mass is about the mean** of the other two.

**(d)** Only a **very few triads** could be found, so most elements could not be placed in this way.

questions.solution_md: Means 81.25 and 80; both agree; the law of triads; too few triads.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: close to the middle and similar properties
Law: groups of three, similar properties

questions.stem_md:
Newlands arranged the first elements in rows of seven in the order of increasing atomic mass: Row 1: Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F. Row 2: Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl. Row 3: K, Ca.

(a) State Newlands' law of octaves. [2]

(b) Name the elements that resemble lithium and the elements that resemble fluorine. [2]

(c) Name the eighth element counting beryllium as the first. [1]

(d) State two limitations of the law. [3]

(e) Why did the noble gases not fit into the arrangement? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** When elements are arranged in order of **increasing atomic mass**, the **eighth element** from any one has properties **similar to the first**.

**(b)** Lithium: **sodium and potassium**. Fluorine: **chlorine**.

**(c)** **Magnesium**.

**(d)** It held good **only up to calcium**; **unlike elements** were placed in the same column; there was **no place for new elements** (any two).

**(e)** The noble gases were **not yet known**, and a new column would break the rule of eight.

questions.solution_md: Every eighth element repeats; Na, K and Cl; magnesium; two limitations; noble gases were unknown.

questions.stem_md:
Mendeleev's table left a gap between zinc and arsenic for an element he called eka-silicon. In the same table tellurium (127.6) is placed before iodine (126.9).

(a) State Mendeleev's periodic law. [2]

(b) Name the element later found in the gap named eka-silicon and state what this discovery showed. [2]

(c) State two merits of Mendeleev's table. [2]

(d) Tellurium is heavier than iodine, yet it is placed before it. Explain why this was done. [2]

(e) Show how the modern periodic law, using the atomic numbers 52 for tellurium and 53 for iodine, removes this anomaly. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The properties of elements are a periodic function of their **atomic masses**.

**(b)** **Germanium**; it showed that the table could **predict** undiscovered elements and their properties.

**(c)** Gaps left and properties predicted; atomic masses of some elements corrected; similar elements grouped (any two).

**(d)** Iodine **resembles chlorine and bromine** and had to be in their group, so the **order of atomic mass was broken**.

**(e)** In the modern law the elements are arranged by **atomic number**: 52 comes before 53, so tellurium precedes iodine **without any exception**.

questions.solution_md: Law with atomic masses; germanium and predictions; two merits; iodine kept with halogens; atomic number order 52 then 53.

questions.stem_md:
The diagram shows the outline of the modern periodic table with five regions lettered A to E.

(a) Name the families of elements in A, B and C. [3]

(b) State the number of valence electrons in the atoms of A and of B. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is the **alkali metals** (group 1), **B** the **halogens** (group 17) and **C** the **noble gases** (group 18).

**(b)** **A:** 1; **B:** 7.

**(c)** **D** is the **transition elements**, in **groups 3 to 12**.

**(d)** **E** shows the **inner transition elements** (lanthanides and actinides); they are set apart so that the table is not too wide.

**(e)** **8**.

questions.solution_md: Alkali metals, halogens, noble gases; 1 and 7; transition elements, groups 3 to 12; inner transition elements; 8.

Four atoms W, X, Y and Z have atomic numbers 3, 11, 16 and 18.

(a) Write the electronic configuration of each atom. [4]

(b) State the period and the group of each. [4]

(c) Which two of the atoms are in the same group? Give a reason for their similar properties. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **W:** 2, 1; **X:** 2, 8, 1; **Y:** 2, 8, 6; **Z:** 2, 8, 8.

questions.stem_md:
A student collects data about three groups. The approximate melting points of the alkali metals are lithium 181 °C, sodium 98 °C and potassium 63 °C. At room temperature chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid.

(a) State the trend in the melting points of the alkali metals down the group. [1]

(b) Why are the alkali metals similar in their chemical properties? [2]

(c) State the trend in reactivity of the alkali metals and give a reason. [2]

(d) Name the family that contains chlorine, bromine and iodine, state its valence electrons and the ion formed. [3]

(e) Explain why argon, neon and helium are unreactive. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The melting point **falls** down the group (181, 98, 63 °C).

**(b)** Each has **one valence electron**, which is lost in reactions.

**(c)** Reactivity **increases** down the group, because the outer electron is **lost more easily** in the larger atoms.

**(d)** The **halogens**, with **7** valence electrons, forming **X⁻** ions.

**(e)** They have **full outer shells** (a duplet in helium, an octet in the others), so they do not react.
